summary: Gives guidelines so protocols can move from one mandatory-to-implement cryptographic algorithm suite to another over time. It discusses algorithm agility and how to choose the algorithms that every implementation must support.

plainLanguage.summary: Every cryptographic algorithm gets weaker as time passes and computing power grows. This document tells protocol designers how to build protocols that can move to a newer algorithm later, and how to choose the small set of algorithms that every implementation must be able to use.

questions: what does should+ mean in an rfc
why are weak algorithms hard to remove
subtitle: How to design protocols so that aging cryptography can be swapped out, and how to pick the algorithms every implementation must support.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic algorithms weaken over time, so every protocol that uses them needs a way to move to a different algorithm without breaking the network.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out guidelines: identify algorithms explicitly, keep a small set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms in a companion document, protect the negotiation itself, and give notice before a change.
tldr.outcome: Protocols designed this way can replace weak algorithms while keeping peers talking. RFC 7696 is an Internet Best Current Practice.

today: RFC 7696 is an Internet Best Current Practice, published in November 2015. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so the guidance stands as written.

sections.title: Why Algorithm Agility Matters
sections.content:
Many IETF protocols use cryptographic algorithms to provide confidentiality, integrity, authentication or digital signature. Peers must support a common set of algorithms for those mechanisms to work. In most cases a combination of compatible algorithms provides the security services needed, and the set in use at a particular time is often called a cryptographic algorithm suite or cipher suite. An algorithm identifier in a protocol may name a single algorithm or a whole suite.

Algorithms age. As new cryptanalysis appears and computing power grows, the work needed to break an algorithm falls, so more attackers can break it. It is unknown how cryptoanalytic attacks will evolve, but it is certain they will improve. Protocol designers therefore have to assume that any algorithm will eventually become obsolete, and protocols need a mechanism to migrate from one suite to another.

Algorithm agility means a protocol can easily move to a more desirable suite over time. For the implementer, that means the code should be modular so new algorithms can be added easily, and there should be a way to measure when deployments have moved away from the old algorithms. For the designer, it means one or more algorithm identifiers must be supported, the set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms will change over time, and a registry of algorithm identifiers will be needed.

Identifiers alone are not enough. People who maintain implementations and operate services have to develop, deploy and reconfigure systems to enable the new algorithms and disable the old ones. Experience shows it is hard to remove or disable weak algorithms, mostly because of interoperability worries, and legacy systems and small devices that cannot support new algorithms add to the problem. People end up living with weak algorithms, sometimes seriously flawed ones, long after experts recommend moving on.
sections.plainLanguage: Cryptographic algorithms get weaker as computers get faster and as researchers find new ways to attack them. A protocol that hard-codes one algorithm has no way out when that happens. A protocol that names its algorithms and can negotiate between them can be updated later without being redesigned.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
An IETF protocol that uses cryptographic algorithms MUST support one or more algorithms or suites, and it MUST include a mechanism to identify which one is in use. The identifier may be carried explicitly in the protocol, or the management mechanism may be enough: for example, an entry in a key table that holds a key value and an algorithm identifier. If the protocol carries no identifier at all, then a new protocol version or some other major change is needed to move from one algorithm to another, so including an identifier is the minimum step towards agility.

Sometimes a combination of a protocol version number and explicit identifiers is right. TLS in RFC 5246 is an example: the version number names the default key derivation function, and the cipher suite identifier names the rest.

Some protocols carry one identifier per algorithm; others carry one identifier for a whole suite. Both approaches are in use, and a designer is encouraged to pick one and use it consistently across a protocol family. Suite identifiers make it easier for the designer to be sure that the algorithm selections are complete and compatible, but they face a combinatoric explosion as new algorithms are defined. Per-algorithm identifiers instead push the work onto implementations, which must decide at run time which combinations are acceptable.

Regardless of the approach, protocols have historically negotiated the symmetric cipher and the cipher mode together so that they are compatible. In IPsec, IKEv2 in RFC 7296 carries separate identifiers for the Authentication Header and the Encapsulating Security Payload. TLS carries cipher suite identifiers. Both are described as fine design choices.

An IANA registry SHOULD be used for these identifiers. Once an identifier is added it should not be changed or removed, but it is desirable to be able to mark an entry as deprecated when implementing it is no longer advisable.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol has to say which algorithm it is using. That can be a name in the protocol itself or in a key table, and it can name one algorithm or name a whole set of them. Either way, the names are registered with IANA and should not be reused.

sections.title: Mandatory-to-Implement Algorithms
sections.content:
BCP 61 in RFC 3365 recognises that peers using cryptographic mechanisms must support a common set of strong algorithms. An IETF protocol that uses cryptography MUST therefore specify one or more strong mandatory-to-implement algorithms or suites. This does not require every deployment to use them, only that they be available to all deployments.

The IETF has to be able to change that set over time, and it is highly desirable to do so without updating the base protocol specification. To that end it is RECOMMENDED that the base specification point at a companion algorithms document, so that one can be updated without necessarily updating the other. That division also lets the base specification move up the standards maturity ladder even when the algorithm document changes often.

The set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms SHOULD be kept small. It will necessarily change over time, and the transition SHOULD happen before the current algorithms have weakened to breaking point.

Protocols that are embedded in other protocols do not set their own mandatory-to-implement algorithms; the system-level protocol does. S/MIME in RFC 5751, for example, uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax in RFC 5652 and specifies the mandatory algorithms itself, not CMS, so that other protocols can use CMS and make different choices.

The algorithm specification MUST identify the key sizes and parameter sizes that are supported. When more than one key size is available, expect the mandatory one to grow over time. Guidance for asymmetric keys is in BCP 86 in RFC 3766, and for symmetric keys in BCP 195 in RFC 7525.

Where possible, authors SHOULD give notice of expected transitions. One way, first used in RFC 4307, is to mark algorithms with SHOULD+, SHOULD- and MUST-. SHOULD+ means the same as SHOULD, but the algorithm is likely to be promoted to a MUST in future. SHOULD- means the same as SHOULD, but the algorithm is likely to be deprecated to a MAY or worse. MUST- means the same as MUST, but the algorithm is expected to be downgraded later, and in the meantime its status can reasonably be expected to remain at least a SHOULD or a SHOULD-.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protocol that uses cryptography must name at least one strong algorithm that all implementations support, and it should keep that list short so the list can change often. Marking an algorithm with a plus or a minus sign tells implementers that the rule for it is about to change.

sections.title: Moving Away from Weak Algorithms
sections.content:
Moving off an old algorithm that turns out to be weak is not straightforward. It is easy to specify a new, better algorithm, and once the new one is widely deployed the old one should no longer be used. But knowledge of what has actually been deployed is always imperfect, so full interoperability with the new algorithm cannot be guaranteed.

Transition is naturally part of the algorithm selection or negotiation mechanism. Protocols traditionally select the best algorithm or suite that all the peers support and that their policies accept. A mechanism is also needed to find out whether the new algorithm has been deployed. The SMIMECapabilities extension in RFC 5751 lets mail user agents share the list of algorithms they are willing to use, in preference order. The DNSSEC EDNS0 option in RFC 6975 measures the acceptance and use of new digital signature algorithms. In the Resource Public Key Infrastructure, BCP 182 in RFC 6916 introduces a second signature algorithm and then phases out the original one.

In the worst case the old algorithm is found to be badly flawed, so that a casual attacker can download a simple script to break it. That has happened when a strong algorithm was used wrongly or with poor key management, which made the whole suite weak. In that situation the protection is badly compromised, and it may be right to refuse the weak suite well before the replacement is widely deployed.

Either way there comes a point when the old algorithm is refused. That can be a single flag day for everyone, or each installation can pick its own date.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing to a new algorithm only works if both ends are ready for it, and nobody knows for certain how widely the new one has been deployed. Protocols therefore need a way to measure what is in use, and there will come a day when the old algorithm has to be switched off, either all at once or one installation at a time.

sections.title: Protecting the Algorithm Negotiation
sections.content:
Cryptographic algorithm selection or negotiation SHOULD be integrity protected. Without that protection the protocol is open to a downgrade attack, where an attacker forces the peers onto a weaker algorithm than they would have chosen. The attempt to move to a new algorithm can itself introduce new opportunities for downgrade attacks.

The transition mechanism has to take into account the algorithm used to protect the integrity of the negotiation itself. If a protocol specifies a single mandatory-to-implement integrity algorithm, that algorithm will eventually be found to be weak. Extra care is needed when a mandatory-to-implement algorithm protects the negotiation of other cryptographic algorithms, because a flaw in it may let an attacker influence the choice of those other algorithms.

The document also notes that protocol designers have traditionally avoided offering more than one way to establish keys, because it makes the security analysis harder. Frameworks such as EAP in RFC 3748 and SASL in RFC 4422 hide much of the detail from the application, so protocols end up supporting several key establishment approaches, and the approach itself becomes negotiable. That is a design challenge, because the negotiation of the key establishment approach has to be protected before it is used to produce keys. A protocol can negotiate an approach, derive an initial key, and then authenticate the negotiation, but if the authentication fails the only recourse is to start the negotiation over from the beginning.
sections.plainLanguage: The part of the protocol where the two sides agree on an algorithm has to be protected itself. If it is not, an attacker can force the weaker algorithm even when both sides would rather use the stronger one.

sections.title: Why Weak Algorithms Persist
sections.content:
Deprecating a cryptographic algorithm is very difficult. People do not like to introduce interoperability problems, even to preserve security, so flawed algorithms are supported far too long. Making the move from old algorithms to new ones easier reduces the impact of legacy software and long support periods, but social pressure is often needed to make the change happen at all.

Implementers have been reluctant to remove deprecated algorithms from server software, and administrators have been reluctant to disable them because they worry that some party will no longer be able to connect. Both want to use the best supported algorithms, but their actions are held back by the wish to preserve connectivity. Some browser vendors have started to show a visible warning when a deprecated algorithm is used, which gives customers a reason to ask for better security.

Transition is particularly hard in Internet infrastructure. The digital signature on the certificate of an intermediate certification authority is often expected to last decades, which holds back the move away from a weak signature algorithm or a short key. Once a long-lived certificate is issued with a particular signature algorithm, many relying parties depend on it, and none of them can stop supporting it without invalidating all the subordinate certificates. In a hierarchy, many subordinate certificates can be affected by the decision to drop support for a weak signature algorithm or its hash function.

Organisations with significant influence can help by coordinating the end of an algorithm suite, which makes the transition easier for their own users and for others.
sections.plainLanguage: Removing a weak algorithm is hard in practice. Servers worry about turning away clients, administrators worry about breaking something, and certificates that last for decades keep an old signature algorithm alive long after experts want it gone.

sections.title: Choosing the Mandatory-to-Implement Algorithms
sections.content:
There is a tradeoff between the number of algorithms a protocol supports and the time it takes to deploy a new one. Ideally two independent sets of mandatory-to-implement algorithms are specified, giving a primary suite and a secondary suite, so that the secondary one is already widely deployed if a flaw turns up in the primary one.

Being able to use an algorithm of one's own choosing looks desirable, but the selection is often better left to experts. Users pick between configuration profiles that experts have defined, and experts need not name every possible alternative. Specifying all possible choices does not make them all available in every implementation. Mandatory-to-implement algorithms MUST have a stable public specification and public documentation that has been well studied, giving significant confidence. The IETF has always preferred unencumbered algorithms, and widely deployed ones have significant benefits. The chosen algorithms need to resist side-channel attacks and meet performance, power and code size requirements on a wide range of platforms. Including too many alternatives adds complexity to selection or negotiation and will likely hamper interoperability, and may hamper security as well. Designers would be prudent to consider whether existing algorithms can be deprecated.

Using the same algorithms and suites across different protocols simplifies implementation when more than one of those protocols runs in the same device or system.

Sometimes more than one mandatory-to-implement algorithm is needed to raise the chance of interoperability across a diverse population. Authenticated encryption, for example, is provided by AES-CCM in RFC 3610 and by AES-GCM. Both are considered secure. AES-CCM is available in the hardware used by many small devices, and AES-GCM is parallelizable and well suited to high-speed devices, so an application needing authenticated encryption might specify one or both.

Too many choices can be harmful. It is easy to specify any algorithm, and once the specification exists it gets implemented and deployed. Even with moderate uptake it is quite hard to remove algorithms, because interoperability with someone is affected, so weaker ciphers stick around far too long. Where several mandatory-to-implement algorithms are specified, they must be diverse, so that a cryptanalytic advance against one does not also affect the others, and the idea is to have a deployed fallback. All of them need to be exercised regularly to ensure a good implementation, which is not always easy, especially when the algorithms require different credentials. Getting several credentials for one installation is an unacceptable burden on administrators, and the advice on how to switch is at best ad hoc and at worst absent.

Picking one true cipher suite can be harmful too. Protocol designers are sometimes misled by the simplicity of a single choice. Since algorithms age, the selection cannot be stable forever. Even the simplest protocol needs a version number to signal which algorithm is in use, and that gives two benefits: the protocol stays simple because there is no negotiation, and administrators make no algorithm-related configuration decisions. But the only way to respond to news that the algorithm has been broken is to update the protocol specification to the next version, implement it, and get it deployed. The first IEEE 802.11 specification included WEP as its only encryption technique, with many protocol details driven by that choice. WEP proved weak, and a very large effort was needed to specify, implement and deploy the replacements, made harder by the design choices tied to the original algorithm and by the desire for backward compatibility. The experience of moving from SHA-1 to SHA-256 shows that the time from specification to widespread use takes more than five years, even when the specification and the implementation were straightforward and prompt.

Some nations specify cryptographic algorithms and require their use through legislation or regulation. These algorithms may not have wide public review and may have limited geographic scope, but the mandate creates a captive market, so they get specified, implemented and deployed. The default server or responder configuration SHOULD disable such algorithms, so that explicit action by an administrator is needed to enable them where they are actually required. For tiny devices with no user interface, that action may only be possible when the device is bought. National algorithms can force an implementer to produce several incompatible product releases for different countries, at a much greater cost than one product using a globally acceptable algorithm, and the situation is worse if the national algorithms impose different requirements on the protocol, its key management or its use of random values.
sections.plainLanguage: Choosing the algorithms is a tradeoff. A small, well-studied, widely deployed set is easier to support, but a single algorithm has nowhere to go when it weakens. The document also advises keeping algorithms that a country requires switched off by default, so that turning them on is a deliberate act.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document gives guidance to working groups and protocol designers. The security of the Internet improves when broken or weak cryptographic algorithms can be replaced easily with strong ones.

From a software point of view, algorithms can often be added and removed without changing the surrounding data structures, parsing routines or state machines. Separating the algorithm code from the rest of the program makes it easier to deal with special concerns such as key exposure and constant-time execution.

Application protocols often use a transport security protocol such as TLS in RFC 5246 or DTLS in RFC 6347. That insulates the application from the details of cryptography, but the application still has to handle the move from unprotected traffic to protected traffic, and the downgrade from encrypted communication to plaintext.

Hardware makes the transition harder in both directions. Many tiny devices cannot update their firmware at all, and even where they can, the devices are often in places that make it inconvenient. High-end data centre equipment may use special-purpose chips for very high performance, so changing the algorithm means replacing the board, at a cost in money and downtime.

Often the algorithm stays strong and the attack is found against the way it is used. In that case a protocol change is probably needed. The order of cryptographic operations in TLS is an example: the protocol originally encrypted after computing the message authentication code, an order known as MAC-then-encrypt, which is no longer considered secure, and RFC 7366 was written to use encrypt-then-MAC instead. Future versions of TLS are expected to use authenticated encryption algorithms exclusively, which would settle the ordering question. After an attack of this kind, updating the algorithms is not likely to be enough; significant protocol changes may be needed. The BEAST attack against TLS caused many sites to turn off modern algorithms in favour of older, clearly weaker ones.

Protocols that protect stored data have their own problem. S/MIME can protect a message kept in a mailbox, and to read that protected data the implementation still needs to support older algorithms even when it no longer uses them for new data.

Supporting too many algorithms can lead to vulnerabilities, because rarely used code tends to hide undetected bugs. Measurements SHOULD be used to find out whether implemented algorithms are actually in use, and future releases should remove those that are not. Unused algorithms or suites SHOULD be marked deprecated in the IANA registry. In short, eliminate the cruft.

Mechanisms for timely updates are needed to deploy a replacement algorithm, and that takes a long time, so the transition process has to begin when practically exploitable flaws become known. Update processes on some devices involve certification, which adds more time, and devices in health or safety systems often need certification before deployment. Embedded systems and SCADA systems often have upgrade cycles stretching over many years, so action is needed quickly if a replacement is to arrive before exploitation techniques become widely available.

The document establishes no new IANA registries and adds no entries to existing ones. It does RECOMMEND a convention for registries of algorithm or suite identifiers: an identifier should not be changed or removed once added, but it should be possible to mark an entry as deprecated when implementing it is no longer advisable.
sections.plainLanguage: Swapping algorithms is not only a protocol matter. Devices may not be updatable, and an attack may be against how a strong algorithm is used rather than the algorithm itself. The advice is to measure which algorithms are really in use, drop the ones that are not, and start the move to a replacement early.
